Judicial Independence, Collegiality, and the Problem of Dissent in Multi-Member Courts  Threats to judicial independence are most commonly viewed as arising either from politically motivated depredations by other branches of government, or from improper inducements or coercion from individuals or groups in the wider society. Both types of threats are external to the court.

/p  Administrative Feasibility Redux: A Reexamination of the Heightened Ascertainability Requirement for Class Certification   Under Rule 23(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, a class action must meet four requirements before it can be certified: numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequacy of representation. But courts infer an antecedent requirement to these four—that of ascertainability, the idea that the court must be able to define the class as an entity that exists prior to allowing it to litigate on behalf of absent parties. While the idea behind this requirement is uncontroversial (surely, a court should ensure that a class exists prior to certifying one), the Third Circuit has staked out an unusually stringent, atextual position, requiring that a putative class present an “administratively feasible” method for identifying its members prior to certification. That requirement, nowhere present in the text or purpose of Rule 23, presents a near-insurmountable barrier to small-dollar consumer class actions, thus undermining the intent of Rule 23 to ensure that such claims can be pursued. Despite predictions that the Third Circuit would back down from its position, and despite at least five circuits’ explicit rejection of the heightened ascertainability requirement, the Supreme Court has yet to weigh in on this glaring rift in class action jurisprudence. After the Eleventh Circuit’s 2021 rejection of the heightened requirement, the time is ripe to once again ask whether this outlier position is defensible.

# Fourth Circuit strikes down West Virginia Daniel's Law in suits against Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis
...
The Fourth Circuit affirmed a ruling that West Virginia's Daniel's Law, which restricts publishing the home addresses and phone numbers of judicial and law enforcement officials, violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments. A former state law enforcement officer had sued Thomson Reuters America, LexisNexis Risk Solutions and other people-search providers under the law. The court said the statute's lack of a notice requirement, which similar laws include, was fatal.

## 1\. Introduction

These consolidated appeals concern the constitutional boundary between protecting public officials from targeted violence and protecting the dissemination of personal information. The Fourth Circuit held that the challenged provision of West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law, W. Va. Code § 5A-8-24(e) (2021), violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments because its restrictions on publishing officials’ home addresses and unpublished telephone numbers were not narrowly tailored.

Michael Jackson, a retired West Virginia law-enforcement officer, brought five putative class actions against companies operating online “people search” services. The defendants were Thomson Reuters America Corporation; Whitepages, Inc.; Thryv, Inc.; PeopleConnect, Inc., and related companies; and LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Inc. Jackson alleged that they published his protected contact information, and that of thousands of other covered officials, without permission.

The court accepted the compelling importance of protecting judicial and law-enforcement personnel. Its objection concerned the statutory means: liability could arise without advance notice or knowledge that the information concerned a protected person. Because publishers could not reliably identify prohibited disclosures, the statute encouraged suppression of otherwise lawful information.

The decision therefore does not establish that officials’ addresses must always remain publicly accessible. webiq.title: Jackson v. LexisNexis — Fourth Circuit struck down West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law disclosure provision – Case Law Wire
webiq.snippet:
Michael Jackson, a retired West Virginia law-enforcement officer, brought five putative class actions against companies offering online people-search services. He alleged that the companies, including LexisNexis Risk Solutions, disclosed his home address and unpublished telephone number, along with comparable information about thousands of other protected officials, without permission and in violation of West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law.

The challenged provision, West Virginia Code § 5A-8-24 (e), prohibited disclosure of protected officials’ home addresses and unpublished telephone numbers under circumstances in which a reasonable person would believe disclosure would expose someone to harassment or a risk of harm. It permitted actual damages of at least $1,000 per violation, punitive damages, attorney’s fees, and equitable relief. The district court dismissed the actions, holding the provision facially unconstitutional because it imposed a content-based restriction on speech that was not narrowly tailored.

The Fourth Circuit affirmed. It held that disclosing addresses and telephone numbers constitutes speech protected by the First Amendment, even though the information consists of factual data. The statute was content based because liability depended on what information was disclosed and whether it concerned a judicial or law-enforcement official rather than another person. Strict scrutiny therefore applied.

The provision imposed liability without requiring knowledge that the disclosed information concerned a protected person and without requiring the protected person first to request removal. Its reasonable-person condition did not meaningfully narrow liability because publishing personal information online inherently creates some exposure to harassment or harm. The resulting risk of automatic liability encouraged speakers to suppress lawful information broadly.

The court accordingly held § 5A-8-24 (e) facially invalid under the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

While all parties, as well as the court, agreed that the law served a compelling state interest of enhancing the safety and security of judicial and law enforcement officials, the court concluded that the law was not narrowly tailored to serve that interest, as it lacked a notice or knowledge requirement.
